notes: Short case stated on London Local Authorities Act 1990 s38; single-vehicle street trading point is clear.

enrichment.short_title: Single car for sale in street held to be unlicensed street trading
key_facts: Mr Michniewicz left an Audi 80 with a for-sale notice in St Ann's Road, Tottenham, an unlicensed street trading area.
Haringey enforcement officers seized the vehicle under section 38 of the London Local Authorities Act 1990.
Haringey Magistrates dismissed the information on the basis that offering one vehicle for sale could not amount to street trading.
The local authority appealed by way of case stated to the High Court.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Case stated from magistrates on whether offering a single motor vehicle for sale in the street requires a street trading licence.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; magistrates were wrong to dismiss the information; matter remitted to continue the hearing.
enrichment.ratio: Under section 38(2)(a) of the London Local Authorities Act 1990, displaying a single article such as a motor car for sale in a street is capable of constituting unlicensed street trading; section 23 confirms street trading need not be regular business, and the statutory presumption in section 38(2) applies unless the defendant shows another purpose.
legal_issues: Whether offering one motor vehicle for sale in a street amounts to street trading under the 1990 Act
Application of the section 38(2) presumption where a for-sale sign is displayed
Whether regularity of trading is required

notes: Child support departure direction threshold and HRA proportionality analysis are fully reasoned.

enrichment.short_title: Child support contact-cost departure direction refused on £15 weekly threshold

statutes_considered.title: Child Support Departure Direction and Consequential Amendments Regulations 1996

key_facts: The claimant, an absent parent living in London, had monthly staying contact with his daughters in Wrexham under a court order.
He applied for a departure direction to reflect contact costs including travel and guest-house expenses totalling about £235.50 per month.
The Secretary of State allowed only travel costs, converting to £14.38 per week, below the £15 special-expenses threshold in Regulation 19.
The Child Support Commissioner refused permission to appeal; the claimant sought judicial review relying on Articles 3, 6, 8 and Protocol 1 Article 1.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of Child Support Commissioner refusals concerning a departure direction for contact costs.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; the mandatory £15 weekly threshold was not met and the human rights challenges failed on proportionality.
enrichment.ratio: Regulation 19 of the 1996 Regulations imposes a mandatory weekly threshold of £15 for special contact expenses before section 28F(1)(a) is satisfied; monthly costs must be converted to weekly amounts under Regulation 3 and cannot be treated as weekly for fairness reasons; although the regime may disincentivise contact, it is a proportionate response to a pressing social need with a wide margin of appreciation.
legal_issues: Whether the £15 threshold in Regulation 19 is mandatory
Whether monthly contact expenses may be treated as weekly special expenses
Whether refusal of a departure direction infringes Articles 8 and Protocol 1 Article 1
Whether section 3 Human Rights Act can rewrite the statutory scheme
linked_authorities: Plumb v Secretary of State for Work and Pensions [2004] EWHC 1125
Campbell v South Northamptonshire DC [2004] EWCA Civ 409

notes: Undue influence appeal turns on Etridge (No 2) and manifest-disadvantage misapplication; ratio is clear.

enrichment.short_title: Option to surrender life tenancy set aside for presumed undue influence
key_facts: Mr Dowsett sold his freehold at Silchester to the Macklins in 1996 for £18,250 and received a rent-free life tenancy.
Planning permission to rebuild his bungalow would lapse unless construction commenced by February 1999.
In January 1999 the Macklins laid foundations and Mr Dowsett signed an option allowing them to terminate his life tenancy for £5,000 if he failed to complete the bungalow within three years.
He did not complete the build; the Macklins sought enforcement when he refused to surrender the life tenancy.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from a High Court decision refusing to set aside a 1999 option agreement on undue influence grounds.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; Mr Dowsett established both prerequisites for presumed undue influence on a prima facie basis.
enrichment.ratio: Following Royal Bank of Scotland v Etridge (No 2), undue influence requires trust and confidence or ascendancy plus a transaction not readily explicable by the parties' relationship; manifest disadvantage is not the correct test; here financial vulnerability and the option to purchase a life tenancy for £5,000 required explanation and the deputy judge wrongly applied a disadvantage-balancing approach.
legal_issues: Whether the Macklins had ascendancy over Mr Dowsett in January 1999
Whether the 1999 option agreement was explicable without undue influence
Correct application of Etridge (No 2) after CIBC Mortgages v Pitt
Whether contractual landlord-tenant adversity precludes a trust relationship
linked_authorities: Royal Bank of Scotland v Etridge (No 2) [2001] UKHL 44
CIBC Mortgages plc v Pitt [1994] 1 AC 200
National Westminster Bank plc v Morgan [1985] AC 686

notes: Local plan reasons challenge under section 287; Miller and Welsh Development Agency principles applied clearly.

enrichment.short_title: Bromsgrove Local Plan quashed for failing to grapple with inspector's ADR recommendation

statutes_considered.title: Town and Country Planning (Development Plan) (England) Regulations 1999

key_facts: Mrs Grant-Nicholas owned about 5 hectares of grazing land at Fiery Hill Road and Kendal Road, Barnt Green.
An independent inspector recommended designating the land as an Area of Development Restraint and redrawing the Green Belt boundary.
Bromsgrove District Council adopted the local plan contrary to that recommendation without detailed reasons.
The council's later responses largely repeated officers' earlier views and did not address the inspector's factual findings.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application under section 287 of the Town and Country Planning Act 1990 to quash part of an adopted local plan.
enrichment.outcome: Relevant part of the Bromsgrove District Local Plan quashed; summary assessed costs of £10,192.88; permission to appeal refused.
enrichment.ratio: Where an inspector makes findings of fact on Green Belt and sustainability issues, the local planning authority must consider the report with an open mind and give reasons that grapple with substantial points; mere repetition of the authority's previous stance is inadequate, and later reasons cannot cure deficient reasons given at the time of adoption.
legal_issues: Whether the council properly considered the inspector's report
Adequacy of reasons for rejecting an ADR designation
Whether inspector findings were value judgments or facts requiring detailed response
Whether later officer comments could rectify earlier deficient reasons
linked_authorities: Miller v Wycombe District Council [1997] JPL 955
Welsh Development Agency v Carmarthenshire County Council [2000] JPL 692
Westminster City Council v Great Portland Estates Plc [1985] AC 661

notes: Accord-and-satisfaction point and adjournment for Piper/Wakefield disclosure are central; procedural posture is complex but captured.

enrichment.short_title: Racehorse stabling settlement appeal adjourned for partnership disclosure
key_facts: Mr Barnett sued Mr Lewis in 1992 for about £10,435 in stabling and training fees for racehorses.
The parties signed a settlement agreement transferring two horses and requiring £2,000 payment in full settlement.
Mr Lewis claimed he paid £2,000 in cash to Andrew Wakefield, said to be Barnett's business partner, but Barnett denied receipt.
A county court recorder entered judgment for the full amended claim in 1997; enforcement led to a charging order and possession proceedings.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Adjourned civil appeal on whether a 1992 settlement ended the original claim and whether fresh evidence on Barnett/Wakefield partnership should be disclosed.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal adjourned; Barnett ordered to disclose Piper/Wakefield litigation documents within 28 days; possession order stayed; mediation encouraged.
enrichment.ratio: A settlement agreement notifying the court that the action was settled replaced the original claim with new contractual obligations; failure to perform did not revive the original proceedings unless a stay had been intended; the Recorder's notes showed only that Barnett was not paid, not that Lewis never paid; partnership/agency evidence remained crucial and disclosure should be restored.
legal_issues: Whether the 1992 agreement operated as accord and satisfaction ending the original claim
Whether non-payment reopened the pleaded debt claim
Admissibility of fresh evidence on Barnett's partnership with Wakefield
Correct interpretation of the recorder's findings on payment

notes: Administration refusal on jurisdiction and purpose is concise and unambiguous.

enrichment.short_title: Administration order refused for property SPV facing disputed winding-up petition
key_facts: AMCD (Property Holdings Ltd) was a special purpose vehicle managing a nearly complete property development for Toha Properties Ltd.
Consultant Mr Gower claimed about £100,000 in fees and served a statutory demand followed by a winding-up petition.
The director applied for an administration order shortly before the petition hearing but did not identify a clear administration purpose.
Estimated assets of £750,000 matched liabilities including a disputed £100,000 debt and a £650,000 directors' loan.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for an administration order in opposition to a pending winding-up petition.
enrichment.outcome: Administration application refused for lack of jurisdiction and because administration was unlikely to achieve its purpose.
enrichment.ratio: Administration requires that the company is or is likely to become unable to pay its debts and that the purpose of administration is reasonably likely to be achieved; where the disputed debt is substantial and balance-sheet insolvency is not established, and where debt recovery from Toha would be no better under an administrator than a liquidator, a last-minute administration application to stave off a petition will be refused.
legal_issues: Whether the company was insolvent on a balance-sheet or cash-flow basis
Whether administration was reasonably likely to achieve its purpose
Whether disputed debt supported winding-up jurisdiction
Whether administration was a tactical response to the petition

notes: Asylum internal-flight and IAT review grounds analysed in detail; extension-of-time refusal is also clear.

enrichment.short_title: Pakistani Ahmadi asylum challenge refused on internal flight alternative
key_facts: Mr Awan, an Ahmadi from Daska in Pakistan, claimed asylum after religious disputes, FIRs, bribes to police, and sectarian killings elsewhere.
A special adjudicator found he could safely relocate internally, notably to Karachi, and dismissed his appeal.
The Immigration Appeal Tribunal refused leave to appeal; Forbes J refused permission for judicial review.
The Court of Appeal considered Sedley LJ's five identified grounds and refused permission to appeal and an extension of time.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for permission to appeal against refusal of permission to seek judicial review of an IAT leave refusal.
enrichment.outcome: Permission to appeal refused; extension of time refused; no basis to review the IAT decision.
enrichment.ratio: An adjudicator need not address every item of evidence expressly if findings on internal relocation and lack of authoritative pursuit cover proclamation and death-threat issues; mischaracterisation of FIR evidence by the IAT was supplementary where the adjudicator treated FIRs as showing reports only; discriminatory restriction on preaching while proceedings are outstanding does not establish Refugee Convention persecution where internal relocation is not unduly harsh.
legal_issues: Whether the adjudicator failed to deal with reasons for leaving Pakistan
Whether the IAT misread findings on First Information Reports
Relevance of section 298(c) Pakistan Penal Code charges
Availability of an internal flight alternative
Whether restriction on religious manifestation amounted to persecution
linked_authorities: AE & FE v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2003] Imm AR 609
R v Secretary of State for the Home Department ex parte Robinson [1998] QB 929
Manzeke v Secretary of State for the Home Department [1997] Imm AR 524
Sayers v Clarke Walker [2002] EWCA Civ 645
Pharis v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2004] EWCA Civ 654

notes: Reserved reasons distinguishing R v B from stale historic buggery convictions are thorough.

enrichment.short_title: Historic buggery convictions upheld despite R v B delay principles

statutes_considered.title: Criminal Justice and Public Order Act 1994

key_facts: The appellant was convicted at Swansea Crown Court of four counts of buggery with a boy under 16 between 1978 and 1989.
The profoundly deaf complainant, related to the appellant like an uncle and nephew, alleged abuse disclosed only after a 2001 arrest.
The judge refused to stay proceedings for delay; the Full Court granted leave only on the relevance of R v B.
The prosecution case rested largely on the complainant's word but included supporting evidence from his mother and the appellant's knowledge of a Haverfordwest toilet.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal with reserved reasons against four historic buggery convictions after partial leave following R v B.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; convictions held safe despite delay and limited corroboration.
enrichment.ratio: Although R v B allows unsafe convictions to be set aside where delay leaves a defendant unable to mount any effective challenge, that residual discretion does not apply where there is some supporting evidence and ample material to cross-examine on inconsistencies, police interview differences, and late-disclosed incidents; juries must be trusted to make allowances for delay after Parliament abolished corroboration warnings.
legal_issues: Application of R v B to stale sexual abuse trials
Whether delay made a fair trial impossible
Whether convictions were unsafe for lack of effective defence
Distinction between consistent and inconsistent complainant evidence on appeal
linked_authorities: R v B [2003] 2 Cr App R 13

notes: Contractual damages for lost yoghurt market over 12 months; quantum reasoning is detailed and appeal dismissed.

enrichment.short_title: Damages upheld for failure to supply single-pot yoghurt for full contract year
key_facts: Collin & Hobson imported ambient yoghurt from Spanish supplier Leche Pascual under a 1998 agreement for single-pot products.
Leche admitted breach after failing to fulfil the first order because of machinery problems.
Collin had lost its Campina supply and could find no alternative supplier for the minimum one-year period.
The judge awarded about £724,353 for lost profits on projected sales of 6.5m branded and 3m own-brand pots, discounted by 25%.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against assessment of damages following trial of preliminary issues on breach and quantum.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; losses for the full 12-month minimum supply period and 25% discount upheld.
enrichment.ratio: Where a supplier knew the buyer could not source equivalent product elsewhere, loss of the entire anticipated market for the contract year was reasonably foreseeable from failure to deliver the first order; starting from historic Campina sales was one factor in a speculative but informed assessment, and a 25% discount adequately reflected commercial uncertainty.
legal_issues: Foreseeability of loss of market for the full contract period
Correct starting point for projected sales volume
Appropriateness of a 25% risk discount
Treatment of Best In own-brand and Londis/Nisa projections

notes: Restrictive covenant injunction on 1963-character general store tobacco display; factual line-drawing is clear.

enrichment.short_title: Supermarket tobacco display restricted under 1963 general-store covenant
key_facts: Mr and Mrs Williams ran a CTN business at No 4 Parkway, Sketty, under a 1964 lease with user covenants.
Mr Kiley operated a supermarket at Nos 6-8 Parkway under a 1963 lease prohibiting use as tobacconist or confectioner.
The court found a building scheme and breach because tobacco and confectionery sales exceeded ancillary general-store sales.
An injunction limited tobacco display to about 1.74 metres of Gallagher counter-top shelving rather than Kiley's much larger display.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against terms of an injunction following preliminary issues on covenant enforceability and breach.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; tobacco display restriction upheld based on 1963 character of a general store.
enrichment.ratio: A covenant permitting grocery and general store use allows some tobacco sales ancillary to that business but not a separate tobacconist trade judged by the character of use in November 1963; where an expert report focused on modern turnover rather than 1963 display norms, the trial judge was entitled to prefer his earlier factual findings and impose shelf-space limits consistent with small 1963 displays.
legal_issues: What quantity or manner of tobacco sales is permitted under a 1963 general-store covenant
Whether injunction terms should follow expert turnover thresholds or historical display size
Whether the judge could reject the joint expert report on injunction wording
Relationship between shelf-space restriction and breach of tobacconist use

confidence.notes: Liability and building scheme were previously decided; this judgment concerns injunction quantification only.
